intro: The first five books of the Bible are called the Torah in Jewish tradition and the Pentateuch, "five scrolls," in Greek. They open with creation and close with Moses looking at a land he will not enter. In between are stories of a flood, a family, an escape, and a mountain, and hundreds of laws about worship, food, courts and neighbors. Jews, Christians and Muslims all know these stories, and each tradition reads them in its own way.

In this unit you will read the Torah as literature and as history. As literature, you will watch how the writers build a scene, repeat a pattern, pun on a name, and leave a question open. As history, you will set the text beside what archaeologists have dug up: a flood tablet from Nineveh, a law stone from Babylon, an Egyptian stele that names Israel. You will learn what those finds can say and what they cannot.

By the end you will be able to tell the two creation accounts apart, compare Noah's flood with the Epic of Gilgamesh, follow the promise from Abraham to Joseph, count the Ten Commandments three ways, and explain how Jewish and Christian readers, and modern scholars, read the same page differently. You will report what the text says and who reads it how, without deciding for anyone what to believe.
bigQuestion: How do the five books of the Torah tell a people's story of beginnings, promise and law, and how have different readers understood the same words?

test.q: Which name for God does Genesis 1 use?
test.why: Genesis 1 uses Elohim. Genesis 2 and 3 switch to "the LORD God," one of the differences readers notice between the accounts.

test.q: What do traditional readers and source critics share when they read Genesis 1 and 2?
choices: The same text with its differences in order and style
The same explanation for the differences
The belief that chapter 2 is later
The view that Moses wrote both
test.why: Both start from the same two chapters. They differ on how to explain the differences: one story told twice, or two sources joined.

test.q: Which detail appears in the Gilgamesh flood but not in Genesis?
choices: Birds sent out to test the water
Gods gathering like flies around a sacrifice
test.why: Tablet XI describes the gods crowding around Utnapishtim's sacrifice. Genesis has one God who promises never to flood the earth again.

test.q: What sign does Genesis 9 give for the covenant with Noah?
test.why: Genesis 9:13 sets the rainbow as the sign. Circumcision is the sign of the covenant with Abraham in Genesis 17.

test.q: Who is the only person in Genesis to give God a name?
test.why: Genesis 16:13 says Hagar named the God who found her by the spring.

test.q: What does Genesis 32 say the name Israel means?
test.why: After wrestling all night, Jacob is named Israel, which the text explains as striving with God and with people.

test.q: What can archaeology say about Abraham, Isaac and Jacob?
choices: It has found their tombs and names
It has shown they never lived
It describes their world but cannot confirm or deny them
It proves they lived in Egypt
test.why: No inscription names the ancestors. Archaeology fills in the Middle Bronze Age setting; historians say the stories cannot be verified either way.

test.q: What does Pharaoh's daughter do in Exodus 2?
choices: Finds Moses in a basket and raises him
test.why: Exodus 2:5-10 says Pharaoh's daughter found the basket, took pity, and named the child Moses.

test.q: How does the King James Version translate God's answer at the burning bush?
test.why: Exodus 3:14 in the KJV reads "I AM THAT I AM." The 1917 JPS leaves the Hebrew untranslated.
Exodus 12 gives the instructions for the lamb, the unleavened bread and the yearly remembrance that is Passover, Pesach.

test.q: In the Protestant and Orthodox count, what is the second commandment?
choices: Thou shalt not make a graven image
I am the LORD thy God
test.why: Reformed Protestants and Orthodox Christians count "no other gods" first and "no graven image" second. Jews and Catholics join them into one.

test.q: Which two law collections both contain a law about a goring ox?
choices: The Covenant Code in Exodus and Hammurabi's laws
test.why: Exodus 21 and Hammurabi's laws, about 1750 BCE, both rule on an ox that gores, one of the closest parallels between them.

test.q: Where does "love thy neighbour as thyself" first appear?
test.why: Leviticus 19:18 is the source. Mark 12 quotes it alongside Deuteronomy 6:5.

test.q: What does the Merneptah Stele show about Israel?
choices: That a people called Israel lived in Canaan by about 1208 BCE
test.why: The stele lists Israel among peoples in Canaan. It says nothing about an escape from Egypt.

test.q: Which describes the Deuteronomy 6:4 translation difference correctly?
choices: KJV and JPS 1917 supply the verb "is" in different places
test.why: The Hebrew has no verb. KJV reads "The LORD our God is one LORD"; JPS 1917 reads "the LORD our God, the LORD is one."

write.prompt: How does the Torah use a story to explain a law? Choose one law and one story, for example Exodus 20:2 and the escape from Egypt, Leviticus 19:34 and Genesis 12, or Deuteronomy 5:15 and Exodus 1. Cite two or three passages by book, chapter and verse. Explain what each says, how the story and the law connect, and how at least two different readers, Jewish, Christian or scholarly, have read them.
tips: Name every passage you use: book, chapter and verse, and the translation.
Attribute each reading: "Jewish tradition reads," "many scholars think," "Christian readers often."
Compare readings; do not rank them or say which is true.
Use the unit's terms: covenant, case law, narrator, etiology, Shema.
Start from what the text says, then move to what it has meant.
